intro_md:
Good morning, Tân! ☀️ **Day 2.** Today is a little easier than Day 1 on purpose: **listening is slower (0.85×)** so your ears can catch up with your eyes.

| When | What | Time |
|---|---|---|
| 🌅 **Morning, 7:45** | Parts 1–2 · Listening | ~40 min |
| 🌙 **Evening, 20:30** | Parts 3–6 · Reading + linking words | ~60 min |
| 🎧 21:40 | Free listening – see **📅 Plan** | ~50 min |

**How to listen (every audio today):**
1. Listen once **without** the transcript. Answer what you can.
2. Listen again **while reading** the transcript.
3. Listen one more time **without** it. Notice how much more you hear.

You'll meet the words from Day 1 again (*although, rather, in other words, be used to, suggest, it takes…*). Don't study them – just notice them.

parts.title: Hope Street: The next morning
parts.md: Nam meets Margaret on the stairs the next morning. Two voices, natural but slow.

listen.text: Morning, Nam! Did you sleep well?
Not really, to be honest. The heating made that noise again at about three o'clock, and then I couldn't get back to sleep.
Oh dear. I told you it always does that. You'll get used to it.
I hope so. I'm not used to sleeping in a new place. And it's so quiet here at night. It's a bit strange.
Quiet? You should hear it on a Friday night, when the students from the house next door come home!
Now, have you eaten anything yet? There's a little café on the corner. It's cheap, and the coffee is good. I suggest going there before work.
That's a good idea. What time does it open?
Seven, I think. And Nam, it takes about twenty minutes to walk to the city centre, so don't be late on your first day.
Twenty minutes? Then I'd better go now. Thanks, Margaret!
Good luck! And take an umbrella. It's going to rain again.

questions.q: Why didn't Nam sleep well?
options: The heating made a noise at night.
The students next door were loud.

questions.q: At about what time did the noise wake him up?
What does Margaret suggest?
options: Going to the café on the corner before work.

questions.q: How long does it take to walk to the city centre?
**Dictation:** type exactly what Nam says, starting with *"I'm not used to…"*
**Dictation:** type Margaret's short sentence starting with *"You'll get…"*

parts.title: The first-night effect
parts.md: A short talk about why we sleep badly in a new place – just like Nam. One speaker, slow and clear.

listen.text:
Have you ever slept badly on your first night in a hotel, or in a new home? If so, you're not alone. Scientists call it the "first-night effect".

For many years, researchers knew about it, but they didn't really understand why it happens. Then, in 2016, a team at Brown University in the United States studied people sleeping in a laboratory. They measured the brain activity of each person, side by side, left and right.

They found something surprising. During deep sleep on the first night, one half of the brain, usually the left half, stayed more awake than the other. It was a bit like a night guard. When the scientists played strange sounds, that half of the brain reacted more, and people woke up more easily.

In other words, the brain was not just sleeping badly. It was keeping watch in an unfamiliar place, just in case something was wrong. Rather than a problem, it may be a kind of protection.

The good news? When people came back to sleep there again, the effect was much weaker. So if you've just moved house, don't worry too much. Your brain simply needs a little time to decide that the new place is safe.

questions.q: What is the talk mainly about?
options: Why people often sleep badly in a new place.
How to choose a good hotel.
Why noise is bad for the brain.

questions.q: Which half of the brain usually stayed more awake on the first night?
The speaker compares that half of the brain to…
According to the speaker, the first-night effect may be…
What happened when people came back to sleep there again?
The speaker says *"**In other words**, the brain was not just sleeping badly."* What does *in other words* do here?
options: It gives the same idea again in a clearer way.
It starts a completely new topic.

questions.q: How much of this talk did you understand on the **first** listen/read (before the transcript or gloss)? Write a number, e.g. 75

parts.title: Hope Street – Episode 2: The Café on the Corner
parts.md:
Read it like a story, without stopping. It should feel easy. <mark>Highlighted</mark> phrases are chunks to notice; **bold** words connect ideas.

> The café on the corner of Hope Street was small and warm. It smelled of coffee and fresh bread, and there were only six tables. A young woman with short red hair was standing behind the counter.
>
> "Morning! What can I get you?" she asked.
>
> "A coffee, please," Nam said. "And… something to eat. I'm not sure what's good."
>
> She smiled. "Then try the bacon sandwich. Everyone says it's the best in Manchester. I'm Jess, <mark>by the way</mark>. I haven't seen you before."
>
> "I'm Nam. I <mark>moved in</mark> yesterday – number fourteen."
>
> "Margaret's building? <mark>Lucky you</mark>. She knows everything about everyone on this street." Jess laughed. "Did the heating wake you up?"
>
> Nam stared at her. "How do you know about the heating?"
>
> "Everyone knows about the heating."
>
> Nam sat by the window with his coffee. Outside, people were walking quickly to work under black umbrellas. He felt tired, **but** he also felt something else – something he hadn't felt yesterday. He <mark>felt a little bit at home</mark>.
>
> The sandwich arrived. Jess was right: it was very good.
>
> **While** he was eating, he checked his phone. There was a message from his new manager, Claire: *"Welcome to the team! See you at 9. Don't worry about being on time today – the trains are terrible."*
>
> Nam looked at the clock. It was 8:15. **Although** Claire said not to worry, he didn't want to be late on his first day. He finished his coffee, said goodbye to Jess and stepped out into the rain.
>
> Twenty minutes later, he was standing outside a tall glass building. His shoes were wet, his hair was wet, and his heart was beating fast. He <mark>took a deep breath</mark> and pushed the door.
>
> "You must be Nam," said a woman with grey glasses. "I'm Claire. Come in – you look like you need another coffee."
>
> Nam laughed. It was only his second day in Manchester, and he was already <mark>getting used to</mark> two things: the rain, and people offering him coffee.

questions.q: Who is Jess, and where does she work?
How does Jess know about the heating?
options: Everyone on the street knows about it.
She heard it from the café.

questions.q: Why does Nam leave the café quickly?
options: Although Claire said not to worry, he didn't want to be late.

questions.q: How does Nam feel in the café? Copy the sentence from the story that shows it.
At the end, Nam is *"getting used to two things"*. What are they, and why is it a little funny?

parts.title: Why do AI chatbots sometimes make things up?
parts.md:
A bit harder (B1+/B2), about a topic you use every day at work. Read once for the main idea, then again slowly. **Bold** words are linking words – watch how they turn the idea.

> If you use AI chatbots, you have probably seen **it** happen. You ask a simple question, and the answer sounds <mark>confident</mark> and well written – **yet** part of it is completely wrong. A book that doesn't exist, a date that never happened, a quote that nobody ever said. People call this a "hallucination".
>
> Why does it happen? It helps to understand what a chatbot is actually doing. A large language model does not look up facts in a list, the way a search engine finds a web page. **Rather**, it <mark>predicts</mark> which words are most likely to come next, based on patterns it learned from huge amounts of text. Most of the time, the most likely words are also the true ones. **However**, when the model doesn't have enough information, it can still produce words that sound right, **even though** they are not.
>
> **In other words**, the chatbot is not lying. It has no <mark>intention</mark> to trick you. It is doing what it was built to do – producing likely-sounding language – in a situation where "likely" and "true" are not the same thing.
>
> Companies are working hard to <mark>reduce</mark> the problem, for example by connecting chatbots to search tools so they can check sources. **Until** it disappears completely, **though**, the best advice is simple: for anything important, check the answer yourself.

**Gloss (only if you need it):**

| Word / phrase | Meaning (simple English) |
|---|---|
| confident | sure of yourself; sounding certain |
| make things up | invent things that are not true |
| predict | say what will probably come next |
| intention | a plan or purpose in your mind |
| reduce | make smaller or less |
| until …, though | but before that happens, … |

questions.q: What is the main idea?
options: Chatbots sometimes give false information because they predict likely words, not facts.
Chatbots are dangerous and should not be used.
Search engines are always better than chatbots.

questions.q: In the first sentence, what does **it** in *"you have probably seen it happen"* refer to? (Tip: the answer comes **after** it.)
*"…sounds confident and well written – **yet** part of it is completely wrong."* Here, **yet** means…
Paragraph 2: *"**Rather**, it predicts which words are most likely to come next…"* What is *Rather* contrasting with? (What does the chatbot NOT do?)
Why does the writer say *"the chatbot is not lying"*?
options: Because it has no intention to trick you.
Because its answers are always true.

questions.q: According to the text, what is the best advice for now?
